prompt: Within one Kafka consumer group, how many consumers can read a given partition at the same time?

options.text: Exactly one consumer per partition
All consumers in the group, in parallel
Up to the topic's replication factor
Any number, as chosen by the producer

explanation: Each partition is assigned to one member of a group, which is what preserves per-partition order. (b) describes separate groups, each reading everything. (c) confuses broker replication with consumption. (d) is wrong: producers don't control consumer assignment.

prompt: How many partitions should the topic have?
scenario: A topic must handle 60,000 messages/s at peak. One consumer handles 3,000 messages/s. Traffic is expected to grow 50% over the next two years, and the team wants per-account ordering.

options.text: At least 30 (20 now × 1.5), plus headroom, keyed by account ID
1 partition, so every account's events keep a single global order
20 exactly, matching today's load, and add partitions as traffic grows
3, one per broker, since more partitions than brokers adds no throughput

explanation: 60,000 ÷ 3,000 = 20 consumers now and about 30 after growth, so at least 30 partitions with some headroom. Keying by account gives the per-account order needed. (b) caps throughput at 3,000/s and gives global order nobody asked for. (c) leaves no headroom, and adding partitions later remaps keys, briefly breaking per-account order. (d) caps the group at 3 consumers; partitions, not brokers, set a group's parallelism.

prompt: With Kafka's default partitioner, where do messages with the same non-null key go?

options.text: Always to the same partition, as long as the partition count doesn't change
Round-robin across all partitions, so load spreads evenly per key
To whichever partition currently has the least data when the message is produced
To a random partition each time, to avoid hot spots on popular keys

explanation: The key is hashed modulo the partition count, so the same key maps to the same partition until the count changes. (b), (c) and (d) would scatter one key's messages and destroy per-key ordering; spreading without per-key order only happens for messages with no key.

prompt: What will adding partitions do to the hot spot?
scenario: A payments topic has 24 partitions keyed by merchant_id. One huge merchant produces 30% of all events, and the consumer for its partition is always behind. The team proposes increasing to 96 partitions.

options.text: Nothing for that merchant: its events all still hash to one partition and one consumer
It spreads the merchant's events across 4 partitions, since each old partition splits in four
It fixes the hot spot, because each partition now carries a quarter of the old traffic
Kafka automatically salts hot keys across the new partitions when the count grows

explanation: One key always maps to one partition, so its 30% share can't shrink by adding partitions. Fixes are a finer key, salting (losing cross-salt order) or a separate topic. (b) and (c) assume one key's events are split, which they aren't: partitions don't split, and a key hashes to exactly one. (d) is false; Kafka has no automatic key salting.

prompt: What happens to existing keyed data when you increase a Kafka topic's partition count?

options.text: Old messages stay put, but new messages for many keys map to different partitions
Kafka moves every old message to its key's new partition in the background
Nothing changes for any key, because Kafka pins each key to its first partition
The topic is deleted and recreated, so retained messages are lost during resize

explanation: hash(key) mod N changes when N changes, and Kafka doesn't migrate existing data, so a key's old and new events can sit in different partitions for a while. (b) is false; no data is moved. (c) is false for most keys: Kafka keeps no key-to-partition pinning, only the hash. (d) is false; it's an online change and existing data stays.

prompt: Which statement about Kafka ordering is accurate?

options.text: Order holds within a partition in write order; there is no order across partitions
All messages in a topic are delivered in global write order across partitions
Order is guaranteed only within a consumer group, and differs between groups
Kafka gives no ordering guarantee at all, even inside a single partition

explanation: Ordering is a per-partition property. (b) is only true for a single-partition topic. (c) mixes up consumer groups with ordering; every group sees the same per-partition order. (d) is too strong; per-partition order is guaranteed.

prompt: Why are some accounts' events processed out of order?
scenario: A topic is keyed by account_id. Each consumer polls 500 messages and submits them all to a 16-thread pool to speed up processing. Occasionally a withdrawal is processed before the deposit that preceded it.

options.text: The thread pool runs one account's messages concurrently; send each key to a fixed thread
Kafka reordered messages inside the partition when the consumer polled in batches
The key should be a random UUID so events spread evenly across all partitions
The group has too few members, so each consumer polls batches too large to order

explanation: Kafka delivered them in order; the unkeyed thread pool threw that order away. Hash each key to a fixed thread to keep per-key order with in-consumer parallelism. (b) is wrong: per-partition order holds, and batching doesn't reorder. (c) would scatter an account's events across partitions, making it worse. (d) is unrelated: batch size doesn't affect order, the concurrent processing does.

scenario: A consumer group on a 6-partition topic is scaled from 6 to 10 consumers to reduce lag.

options.text: No improvement: 6 consumers get one partition each and 4 sit idle
Throughput rises by about two thirds, since there are 10 consumers instead of 6
Each partition is split between consumers, so all 10 share the load
The 4 extra consumers form a second group automatically and share the load

explanation: Partition count caps a group's parallelism. (b) assumes the extra consumers get work. (c) is false: a partition is never shared within a group. (d) is false: group membership comes from the group ID the consumer is configured with.

prompt: Which of these trigger a Kafka consumer group rebalance? Select all that apply.

options.text: A new consumer with the same group ID joins
A consumer takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms between polls
Partitions are added to the subscribed topic
A producer sends a message with a new key

explanation: Joins (a), consumers presumed dead for not polling in time (b) and partition-count changes (c) all force reassignment. (d) only affects which partition a message goes to; it doesn't change group membership.

prompt: Which change most directly reduces disruption during deploys?
scenario: Every rolling deploy of a 30-consumer group causes many rebalances; each pauses all consumption for several seconds and produces a burst of duplicate processing. Consumers restart within 20 seconds.

options.text: Static membership plus cooperative rebalancing, and committing offsets on revoke
Increase the partition count so each rebalance moves less data per consumer
Switch producers to acks=0 so publishing isn't held up while consumers rebalance
Disable offset commits so restarted consumers never conflict over committed offsets

explanation: Static membership (group.instance.id) lets a quickly-restarted consumer reclaim its partitions without a rebalance; cooperative rebalancing moves only what must move; committing on revoke cuts duplicates. (b) makes rebalances move more partitions, not less. (c) weakens producer durability and doesn't affect consumers. (d) makes every restart reprocess from the last commit, causing more duplicates.

prompt: How long until the group catches up?
scenario: After an outage, lag is 900,000 messages. Producers write 12,000 messages/s and the group processes 18,000 messages/s at full speed.

options.text: 150 seconds
50 seconds
75 seconds
It never catches up

explanation: The backlog shrinks at 18,000 − 12,000 = 6,000/s, so 900,000 ÷ 6,000 = 150 s. (b) divides by 18,000, ignoring new arrivals. (c) divides by 12,000, which is the arrival rate, not the catch-up rate. (d) would be true only if processing were slower than arrivals.

prompt: Why alert on time lag rather than lag in messages?

options.text: Time lag (oldest unprocessed message's age) matches user delay at any throughput
Message lag can't be measured in Kafka, since offsets aren't exposed to clients
Time lag is always the smaller number, so alerts fire less often and are less noisy
Message lag only exists for SQS queues, while Kafka reports lag in seconds

explanation: 50,000 messages is negligible at 100,000/s and severe at 10/s; time lag captures what users feel. (b) is false: it's log-end offset minus committed offset. (c) is meaningless since the units differ. (d) is false: Kafka reports per-partition message lag.
